title: Beta check-in: Quantization Profile rollout (Acme AI)
summary: Acme AI shared early results from enabling a quantization profile on one production-like route. They’re seeing ~18–22% lower cost/token and slightly improved throughput on H100, with p95 latency roughly flat. However, they reported an edge-case quality regression: structured JSON outputs occasionally missing a required key under a specific prompt template and low temperature. Redwood reviewed monitoring signals (fallback_rate, quant_profile_id tags, errors) and agreed on a short-term mitigation (pin profile version + narrow rollout) while Applied ML investigates. Next steps include Acme providing 6–10 concrete failing request IDs, Redwood running targeted A/B evals on the prompt set, and setting explicit rollback criteria for the next canary step.
topics: Monitoring and dashboards: quant_profile_id tagging, applied vs fallback, fallback_rate thresholds
Early cost/token and latency deltas on Dedicated H100 pool
Edge-case regression on structured output (missing field / invalid JSON) under specific template
Route-level configuration hygiene: pinning profile version vs aliases, region/tier constraints
Roll-forward/rollback plan (route disable + global kill switch) and oncall expectations
next_steps: Acme to send failing request IDs + prompts/output diffs (sanitized) and confirm exact route + model variant
Redwood to reproduce with the same profile/version and run route-level A/B eval on Acme’s template family
Redwood to review traces to confirm applied vs fallback and whether any burst capacity used different GPU SKU
Agree on updated rollout plan: keep to 5% canary until regression understood; define rollback thresholds
Schedule next beta check-in after Redwood shares findings (target early next week)
action_items: Acme (Rina) - Share 6–10 failing examples: request_id, timestamp, route name, expected vs actual JSON, and whether tool/structured output was enabled - Due 2025-03-06
Acme (Samir) - Confirm which regions/tier are in play (Dedicated only vs any burst/hosted spillover) and provide GPU SKU info from their side if available - Due 2025-03-06
Redwood (Jonas Weber) - Run a targeted A/B eval on the reported prompt template family using baseline vs the exact quant_profile_id and quantify delta with confidence intervals - Due 2025-03-07
Redwood (Chloe Martin) - Verify audit log entries for the route toggle changes and ensure Acme can view change history in Console (RBAC) - Due 2025-03-07
Redwood (Connor O'Brien) - Share recommended alert thresholds for fallback_rate and a rollback checklist for Acme’s canary (route disable + verify recovery) - Due 2025-03-07
Redwood (Markus Klein) - Coordinate a short technical follow-up if repro points to structured output mode (JSON schema) interaction and bring Runtime/Applied ML if needed - Due 2025-03-10
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-03-05
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 37 min
Customer: Acme AI
Redwood: Miguel Santos (CSM), Markus Klein (Solutions), Chloe Martin (Console/Tooling), Jonas Weber (Perf/Evals), Connor O'Brien (Release/SRE)

Auto Summary (generated)
- Checked beta rollout status for Quantization Profile Library enablement on a single Acme route.
- Reviewed observed cost/token and latency deltas and monitoring approach.
- Discussed a reported edge-case quality regression in structured output responses.
- Aligned on containment, next steps, and gating criteria before increasing traffic.


[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, I think we’re good. Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Goal today is quick beta check-in on the quant profile rollout. Rina, I saw your note about an edge case regression—def want to dig into that, plus look at the monitoring and early numbers.

[00:16] Rina Shah: Yep. Thanks Miguel. We’re generally happy with the cost improvement, but we hit something weird with JSON responses. Not constant, but enough that we paused going beyond five percent.

[00:28] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Also just to set context, we’re talking about route-level enablement only, right? Like you toggled it on for one route in staging/prod-like.

[00:36] Rina Shah: Yeah, route “chat-prod-canary” on the dedicated cluster. Model is the 70B instruct variant, the x1 one you recommended. Sorry I don’t have the exact internal name in front of me.

[00:48] Chloe Martin: No worries. If you can paste the route ID or the route slug later that’s enough. We can look in the audit log too, if your RBAC view is enabled.

[00:58] Samir Gupta: I can pull it. Also we’re looking at your dashboard panels—there’s one called fallback_rate? We’re trying to interpret it. It’s low but not zero.

[01:09] Connor O'Brien: Yep. Fallback rate is “requested quant profile but runtime applied baseline” basically. Usually incompatibility checks (hardware, context length, whatever) or profile disabled by a guardrail. For dedicated, it should be close to zero unless there’s some burst or mixed SKU in the pool.

[01:28] Evan Cole: That’s what we were wondering. Our dedicated pool is H100s, but we do have a setting where overflow can go to a smaller pool when autoscale lags. I need to check what GPU that is.

[01:39] Markus Klein: That could explain it. Some profiles are constrained to H100 / Hopper only, especially the mixed FP8/INT8 ones.

[01:47] Jonas Weber: And if you’re seeing fallback, the “quant_profile_id” tag in logs should show applied vs fallback, if you have trace sampling on.

[01:56] Rina Shah: We do, kind of. We see “quant_profile_id=qp_…” sometimes, and sometimes it’s blank. That’s the applied vs not applied.

[02:05] Chloe Martin: Right—blank or “disabled” depending on the exporter. There’s also a resolution outcome field that should be “applied” or “fallback” in recent builds.

[02:16] Miguel Santos: Before we go deep into the regression, can you share the early results? You mentioned cost improvements.

[02:24] Rina Shah: Sure. On canary, our average tokens per request is around 1.2k output, 900-ish input. With the profile on, we’re seeing about 18 to 22 percent lower cost per output token, and throughput is a bit better. Latency p95 is basically flat, maybe a few ms worse in one slice.

[02:44] Jonas Weber: That’s consistent with what we saw in the lab for that model on H100. Did you notice any VRAM pressure or OOMs?

[02:52] Evan Cole: No OOM. We did see one spike in 5xx last week, but I think that was the metadata fetch thing you all had. It wasn’t persistent.

[03:01] Connor O'Brien: Yeah that was a known incident on our side—registry fetch retries causing noise. We rolled out caching and rate limiting. You should be on the fixed build now.

[03:12] Samir Gupta: Cool. For monitoring: we’re watching error rate, p95, and we added a panel by quant_profile_id. The question is: what’s a reasonable alert threshold on fallback_rate? Right now it’s around 0.6%.

[03:28] Connor O'Brien: For a controlled canary, I’d want <1% ideally, but also understand why. If it’s overflow to a different SKU, it’s expected, but it undermines the experiment because you’re mixing baseline and quant in the cohort.

[03:43] Rina Shah: Exactly.

[03:45] Miguel Santos: Okay, let’s talk about the regression. Tess, you flagged it too, right?

[03:50] Tess Morgan: Yeah. So we use structured output—like “return JSON with keys: answer, citations, confidence”. Under baseline, it’s stable. With quant enabled, occasionally, maybe 1 in 200-ish, the “citations” field is missing or the JSON is slightly malformed. It’s not random prompts; it’s a specific template we use for knowledge base queries.

[04:13] Jonas Weber: Missing a key, or extra trailing text after the JSON?

[04:18] Tess Morgan: Both. Most common is missing “confidence”. Sometimes it returns “confidence:” but not as a key-value, like it drops the braces. It’s subtle.

[04:29] Markus Klein: And this is temperature zero?

[04:32] Tess Morgan: We’re at 0.1, top_p 1. max_tokens 256. And we set a strict JSON schema in your request. Sorry, I might be mixing terms, but it’s the structured output mode.

[04:46] Chloe Martin: That’s helpful. On our side it’s “structured_output” with a JSON schema. There are known sensitivity points: very small max_tokens and low temperature can amplify small logit differences.

[04:58] Rina Shah: Which we can accept, but we need it to not break the parser. Our downstream assumes valid JSON.

[05:06] Miguel Santos: Totally.

[05:09] Jonas Weber: Do you have example request IDs? That’s the fastest way for us to look at exact logits? Well not logits, but at least the trace and the quant profile resolution.

[05:18] Rina Shah: We have two right now. I can pull more. The thing is our privacy policy—can we send you the full prompt?

[05:26] Markus Klein: You can sanitize, or just send the shape. Even a redacted prompt with the same template structure can reproduce.

[05:34] Chloe Martin: Also you can send the request_id and timestamp and we can see the route config, profile applied, and model version. We won’t see your full prompt unless you have payload logging enabled (which I don’t think you do).

[05:47] Samir Gupta: We do not log the prompt to you. Correct.

[05:50] Connor O'Brien: Good.

[05:52] Jonas Weber: Then send request_id + time window. We can check: quant_profile_id, applied/fallback, context length, stop reasons, and any structured output validation errors on our side.

[06:05] Tess Morgan: Do you have a metric for “structured output invalid”? We didn’t see an explicit one.

[06:10] Chloe Martin: There is an error code when the schema validator fails, but it’s not always emitted if your client is doing the validation. In the Console we show “response_format_errors” for some tenants. I need to confirm if it’s enabled for you.

[06:26] Miguel Santos: We can follow up on that. For now, you’re catching it client-side.

[06:32] Rina Shah: Yes, we parse and reject.

[06:36] Jonas Weber: Ok. Another question: are you using the profile ref as “recommended/latest” or are you pinned to a specific version? Because we’ve seen confusion where alias changes can shift behavior.

[06:48] Evan Cole: I think we used “recommended”. That’s what the Console offered.

[06:52] Chloe Martin: For beta, we generally prefer pinning. “Recommended” is useful, but it can move when we publish a new profile version. We try not to change it silently, but there’s still risk.

[07:06] Markus Klein: We can help you pin to qp_<id>@<version> so you know it’s stable during your eval.

[07:12] Rina Shah: That would be great.

[07:15] Connor O'Brien: And it’s better for rollback—if you see a regression, you can flip back to “default” or baseline and be sure what changed.

[07:25] Miguel Santos: So containment-wise: you paused at 5% canary, correct?

[07:29] Rina Shah: Yep. We didn’t disable entirely, just didn’t ramp.

[07:33] Samir Gupta: And we set an alert: if invalid JSON > 0.2% for 10 minutes, we rollback. But it’s hard because we only sample some responses.

[07:45] Jonas Weber: Understood. For our gating, we can run offline A/B on your template if you give us a redacted set of prompts—like 200 examples. Then we can estimate the failure rate statistically.

[08:00] Tess Morgan: We can provide some, but it’ll take a day to sanitize.

[08:05] Miguel Santos: That’s fine.

[08:07] Markus Klein: Also, one more angle: does this happen only when the request is longer? Like near the context limit.

[08:13] Tess Morgan: Not near the max. Usually smaller contexts. But it does happen more when the citations list is long.

[08:21] Jonas Weber: That could be a decode stability issue. Some INT8 weight-only profiles can shift probability mass and you get earlier stop token or formatting drift.

[08:31] Chloe Martin: We also have a known caveat in one profile version around “structured output + forced keys”. I’m not sure if it’s the same one, but we should check your exact quant_profile_id.

[08:43] Rina Shah: That’s basically what we’re afraid of.

[08:46] Connor O'Brien: The good news is the feature is fully reversible. You can disable at route-level immediately, and we have a kill switch platform-wide, but you shouldn’t need that.

[08:56] Samir Gupta: Can we talk rollback steps? Like what to verify.

[09:00] Connor O'Brien: Sure. Step 1: set quantization_profile_ref to “default” for the route. Step 2: watch quant_profile_id in traces go to “disabled” and fallback_rate goes to zero (or not applicable). Step 3: confirm p95 and error rate return to baseline. If you still see issues, then it’s not the profile.

[09:20] Miguel Santos: We’ll send that as a checklist after.

[09:23] Evan Cole: One question: if we disable, does it take effect instantly? Or is there config propagation time.

[09:28] Chloe Martin: Usually under a minute, depending on cache TTL in the control plane and your edge region. Dedicated tends to be faster.

[09:37] Markus Klein: And there’s an audit event for the change: who toggled, when, from what to what.

[09:43] Rina Shah: Good.

[09:45] Miguel Santos: Going back to monitoring: Rina you said cost/token improved about 20%. Any changes in tail latency?

[09:52] Rina Shah: p95 stayed around 780ms for our test. p99 is noisy; sometimes 2.1s vs 1.9s. Hard to say.

[10:02] Jonas Weber: If you can split by “applied” vs “fallback”, that can explain tail. Mixed behavior can produce weird aggregates.

[10:09] Samir Gupta: We can do that.

[10:11] Evan Cole: Another thought: when overflow happens, it’s L40S I believe. Could cause fallback, yes.

[10:18] Connor O'Brien: Yep. If the profile has a hardware constraint, policy engine should fallback cleanly. It shouldn’t loop. There was a rare loop bug we fixed earlier, but you’d see repeated resolution attempts. Are you seeing that?

[10:31] Samir Gupta: Not that I can tell.

[10:33] Chloe Martin: We can check by looking at the “resolution_outcome” field; loops were mostly visible as repeated “incompatible” warnings.

[10:41] Miguel Santos: Ok. Let’s agree on what we need to debug regression. Jonas, what’s your ask?

[10:47] Jonas Weber: Minimum: 6 to 10 request IDs where it happened, with timestamps and route. If possible: the schema you pass (the JSON schema), and whether you’re using tool calling or just response_format. Then I’ll run an internal reproduction and also run an A/B eval with a sanitized prompt set.

[11:08] Tess Morgan: We can share the schema. It’s simple.

[11:11] Rina Shah: And request IDs, yes.

[11:14] Markus Klein: Also confirm: model version pinned? If not, we’ll help pin to a specific profile version as containment.

[11:22] Evan Cole: We can do that today.

[11:24] Chloe Martin: If you want, I can jump on after this call and walk through Console. Sometimes it’s easier than API.

[11:31] Rina Shah: Please.

[11:33] Miguel Santos: Great. On our side, we should probably recommend keeping canary at 5% until we know whether this is profile-specific or general quant sensitivity for your template.

[11:43] Rina Shah: Agreed.

[11:44] Connor O'Brien: And set explicit rollback thresholds. Like: invalid JSON > X% or latency p95 increases > Y% for Z minutes.

[11:53] Samir Gupta: For fallback_rate, should we alarm?

[11:56] Connor O'Brien: I’d at least alert at >2% sustained. But again, interpret with overflow. If you can constrain canary to pure H100, that’ll be cleaner.

[12:07] Evan Cole: We can probably temporarily disable overflow for canary route.

[12:11] Markus Klein: That would help isolate.

[12:14] Jonas Weber: Yep, because otherwise the cohort is not apples-to-apples.

[12:18] Miguel Santos: Ok. Quick check: any other issues? Like quality drift not related to JSON.

[12:24] Tess Morgan: We saw one weird answer about policy. But could be normal model variance.

[12:29] Rina Shah: Main one is structured output invalid.

[12:33] Chloe Martin: Understood.

[12:35] Markus Klein: Did you compare to other providers? You mentioned Together earlier in the thread.

[12:39] Rina Shah: Yeah, we tested Together’s quantized endpoint. Cost was good but we lacked route-level control and auditability. That’s why we’re here.

[12:49] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[12:51] Samir Gupta: And for AWS Bedrock, it’s just pricey for our workload.

[12:55] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[12:57] Jonas Weber: While we have you—does your template include long lists of citations? Because that can trigger high repetition penalty effects.

[13:05] Tess Morgan: It’s a list of doc IDs and snippets, yes.

[13:08] Jonas Weber: Ok. If it’s “missing key”, sometimes it’s because the model stops early. What stop reason do you see? length? stop token?

[13:18] Tess Morgan: Usually “stop”, not “length”.

[13:22] Jonas Weber: Interesting. That implies it’s emitting a stop sequence earlier. We can inspect if your stop sequences include “\n\n” or “}”.

[13:31] Tess Morgan: We do include “}” sometimes to try to force closure.

[13:36] Chloe Martin: That can be tricky. If you stop on “}” you can get a valid brace but missing fields. The schema mode usually handles it, but depends.

[13:45] Rina Shah: We added it as a hack, to be honest.

[13:48] Markus Klein: That might be the interaction. Quant might slightly change when “}” appears.

[13:53] Jonas Weber: Yep. In eval, we can test removing that stop sequence and letting schema enforcement handle it.

[14:01] Tess Morgan: That’s a good suggestion.

[14:03] Miguel Santos: Great, capture that as an experiment.

[14:06] Connor O'Brien: And just to clarify, schema enforcement on our side is best-effort—it’s not a hard guarantee in all modes yet, which is why we always recommend client validation.

[14:16] Rina Shah: Yep.

[14:18] Chloe Martin: For beta, we’re adding clearer errors when incompatible or when structured output fails. But that’s next sprint.

[14:27] Miguel Santos: Ok, we’re at about halfway. Let’s do a quick recap of decisions.

[14:33] Miguel Santos: 1) Keep canary at 5%. 2) Pin the quant profile version (no “recommended” alias) for the canary route. 3) Acme sends request IDs and schema + maybe redacted prompt set. 4) Redwood runs A/B eval and trace analysis. 5) We tighten canary isolation—try to avoid overflow onto L40S.

[14:54] Rina Shah: Yep.

[14:55] Evan Cole: Yes.

[14:57] Samir Gupta: Good.

[14:59] Jonas Weber: Works.

[15:01] Chloe Martin: I’ll help with pinning and the audit log view.

[15:04] Connor O'Brien: I’ll send monitoring thresholds and rollback checklist.

[15:08] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[15:11] (brief crosstalk)

[15:13] Markus Klein: One more detail: can you confirm the model variant? Is it llama 3.1 70B instruct x1, or the 8B? I just want to make sure.

[15:22] Rina Shah: 70B. The route is for our main assistant.

[15:26] Markus Klein: Great.

[15:28] Jonas Weber: And the quant method—do you know if it’s int8 weights only or mixed fp8?

[15:33] Rina Shah: I don’t. Console just said “H100 optimized”.

[15:38] Chloe Martin: Likely mixed FP8 activations + INT8 weights, but I’ll confirm the exact profile metadata once we pin it.

[15:46] Tess Morgan: Are there other profiles we could try that are safer for quality, even if savings is less?

[15:52] Jonas Weber: Possibly. There’s a more conservative profile—weight-only int8, no activation quant. Savings is smaller, but tends to preserve formatting better. That’s something we can propose after we analyze.

[16:05] Miguel Santos: Good call.

[16:07] Samir Gupta: Can we also get a compatibility matrix? We’ve been guessing what works on which GPU.

[16:12] Markus Klein: Yep, we have an internal doc and customer-facing one in progress. For now, the profile metadata includes hardware constraints, but it’s not super discoverable. We can share a summary for your environment.

[16:26] Evan Cole: That would help a lot.

[16:29] Chloe Martin: In the Console UI, there’s supposed to be a warning if the route spans unsupported regions/SKUs. If you didn’t see it, maybe it’s not enabled for your tenant yet.

[16:39] Rina Shah: I did see a yellow warning but it was vague.

[16:42] Chloe Martin: Got it. We’re improving the error message to say like “Not supported on L40S” explicitly.

[16:50] Connor O'Brien: Yeah, we shipped improved incompatibility messages recently, but might not be in your console build.

[16:58] Miguel Santos: Ok.

[17:00] Tess Morgan: Another question: is this deterministic? Like if we rerun the same prompt, do we always get the same output? Because we saw some variance.

[17:07] Jonas Weber: Determinism is “as deterministic as baseline”. Quant can change outcomes, but within a given mode, if you set seed (if supported) and same sampling params, it should be stable. GPU kernels and batching can still introduce nondeterminism at low level. We aim to be consistent but not bitwise identical.

[17:26] Rina Shah: That’s acceptable, but we need “valid JSON” consistent.

[17:30] Jonas Weber: 100%.

[17:33] Markus Klein: For your use case, we may recommend a slightly higher temperature? ironically sometimes helps formatting, but we’ll test.

[17:42] Tess Morgan: Interesting.

[17:44] Miguel Santos: Okay, we’re nearing time. Anything else to cover?

[17:50] Samir Gupta: Not really. Just please send the rollback steps and thresholds.

[17:54] Connor O'Brien: Will do.

[17:56] Chloe Martin: And I’ll schedule a 20-min follow up with Rina/Evan to pin the profile version and confirm RBAC for audit logs.

[18:04] Rina Shah: Great.

[18:06] Miguel Santos: Cool. Jonas, when can you share initial findings?

[18:10] Jonas Weber: If I get request IDs tomorrow morning, I can likely have a preliminary analysis by Friday, and A/B eval by end of day Friday or Monday depending on sanitized prompt set size.

[18:23] Rina Shah: We’ll send by tomorrow.

[18:26] Miguel Santos: Perfect. Thanks all.

[18:29] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[18:30] (call ends)
